source.title: LoRA's Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; it is a preprint under review.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests rank- and width-based risk curves, then refines the double-descent account by distinguishing recovery relative to a curve's own valley from performance relative to module-matched dense fine-tuning. It also reports settings where the curve changes or does not show the same recovery.
record.gate_note: Rows below record the study's own capacity, data-size, noise, and optimization results. Cited results from prior work are excluded. The epoch-budget comparison changes the rank curve across training durations; it does not measure a test-error curve across epochs. The paper does not test a multiple-peak curve.
record.test_reason: The study measures capacity–risk curves and qualifies their interpretation in adapter fine-tuning: interpolation and peak locations separate, the visible descent depends on sweep range, and recovery relative to a valley differs from matching dense fine-tuning. It also reports width controls, data-size effects, and noise and regularization dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that sufficiently extended LoRA rank sweeps can exhibit a second descent, while no measured post-peak parameter-saving rank matches module-matched dense risk. DeiT-Tiny first passes equivalence at r=3d, four times dense's projection-weight count, under the shared learning rate. They show that optimization coordinates can move risk within a fixed update class, while leaving the precise cause of ordinary LoRA's residual gap open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses LoRA rank sweeps and module-matched dense fine-tuning, plus width and adapter-family comparisons, on pretrained vision and language systems and from-scratch controls. It is not a reproduction of the original experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The rank-curve peak shifts with training budget; label-noise rate changes cliff depth; clean labels flatten the curve; model family changes whether a cliff or second descent appears; sweep endpoint changes whether a second descent is visible; reference choice (pre-peak valley versus dense fine-tuning) changes the assessment; validation-based hyperparameter selection shrinks the cliff by selecting checkpoints before interpolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-peak parameter-saving LoRA ranks remain above module-matched dense risk; DeiT-Tiny first passes shared-rate equivalence at r=3d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A second descent in adapter risk need not match dense fine-tuning while retaining parameter savings.

fits_no_version.finding: Stable rank grows sublinearly with nominal rank, and training NLL correlates more closely with test NLL than nominal rank does.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nominal adapter rank can poorly summarize learned-update complexity and noisy-label fit.

fits_no_version.finding: Frozen-factor spectrum changes risk at a fixed update class; update-space optimization removes this dependence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization coordinates can affect generalization even when expressible updates are unchanged.

record.problems: The study reports small seed counts for several comparisons; some three-seed resampling intervals are explicitly descriptive. The data-size arms at n=2,500 and n=10,000 use two seeds. Dense equivalence at 3d on DeiT-Tiny is established only under the shared learning rate. Test NLL is the primary outcome, and the study notes accuracy can diverge from NLL at larger ranks. The paper does not establish sample-size interpolation status for each arm or a common effective-complexity predictor across axes.
record.rows_left_out: No reported claim-relevant results were omitted from the selected rows. The many per-rank values for the Qwen2.5-7B sweep are retained as one rank-sweep row, as are dense-axis sweeps with a reported overall shape and recovery.

untested.parts: Broad generalization beyond the sampled architectures, tasks, training budgets, and capacity axes.
A fall-rise-fall test-risk curve over epochs at fixed model capacity.
Interpolation status across every sample-size arm, uncertainty for the reported sample-size contrasts, and generality beyond this fine-tuning setting.
Universality across model classes; the study covers deep networks and one warm-start linear model.
Prediction of peak locations across size, epoch, and sample axes by one effective model complexity measure. Stable-rank measurements and risk correlations do not establish this.
Triple or multiple descent, a variance decomposition, and disappearance of double descent under optimally tuned regularization. The finite searches do not establish optimality.
Replotting risk against an appropriate effective parameter count and demonstrating an ordinary U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Warm-start linear regression theory and simulations: p=2000, n=200, 16 trials; interpolation divergence, second descent, noise dependence, and a prior-quality threshold for finishing below the valley.
Human-label-noise rank sweep: NLL 1.743±0.017 at r=1, 2.408±0.020 at r=64, and 2.350±0.027 at r=384; interpolation begins at r=24. This extends the noise setting beyond synthetic corruption.

Other sample-size contrasts: from 5,000 to 10,000 examples NLL rises from 2.102 to 2.168 at r=64 and from 2.069 to 2.086 at r=192, while declining at r=1 and r=8. The non-main arms use two seeds without reported intervals.

Long-budget rank tails: at 80 epochs fixed-scale NLL falls from 2.351 at r=64 to 2.192 at r=384; at 160 epochs it falls from 2.676 to 2.460. Standard scaling also retains descending tails after longer training.
Augmentation reduces cliff amplitude but the sampled augmented curve has no post-peak descent, a distinct condition not captured by the noise-rate row.

The calibrated noisy-label cliff retains 83% of its amplitude: calibrated NLL is 1.535 at r=1, 1.979 at r=64, and 1.932 at r=192. This checks whether the measured risk shape is primarily miscalibration.

record.verdict_notes: Only supplied text was used. V5 and V7 receive no verdict because their defining predictions are not tested. Returning below the pre-peak valley, matching dense risk, and retaining parameter savings are stronger requirements than V1 or V4 states. Missing-text verdicts use empty row_ids pending extraction.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests width sweeps from scratch and several fine-tuning capacity axes, but not a broad sweep over conventional model sizes or architectures.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported; changing the training budget and observing a rank-curve peak shift is not an epoch-wise curve test.
Data-size results are reported at selected ranks; interpolation status is not separately established at each sample size.
The study covers selected deep-network, adapter, and dense fine-tuning axes, not all model classes or a universal risk curve.
Stable rank and training NLL are examined in LoRA runs, but no single complexity measure is validated as predicting peak locations across size, epoch, and sample axes.
Noise-rate effects and model-selection/weight-decay settings are examined. Triple or multiple descent and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization while interpolating are not tested.
The paper critiques raw parameter counting and measures stable rank, but does not show that an appropriate effective-parameter count converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.
